The matrix died, so these nails will not grow back at all
Over-filing or ripping product damaged the keratin plate
Skipping base coat from now on will let the plate thicken

explanation: Peeling, paper-thin plates right after removal are almost always mechanical damage to existing keratin — over-filing, prying, or forced soak-off — not a dead matrix. distractorExplanations.b: The matrix sits under the proximal fold; surface peeling after removal is plate damage, not matrix death.
distractorExplanations.d: Base coat protects a thinned plate; skipping it does not rebuild keratin lost to over-filing.

prompt: A lacquer bottle is labeled “5-free.” A client with a past polish allergy asks if that means the product is medically hypoallergenic. What should you say?

options.text: 5-free means the bottle contains no chemicals at all
5-free is FDA pre-approval that the polish cannot cause allergy
It omits some listed ingredients; it is not a medical clearance
5-free lacquer can replace acid primer under acrylic overlays

explanation: “3-free” or “5-free” is marketing that certain named ingredients (often toluene, formaldehyde, DBP, and similar) were left out. Every polish is still a chemical mixture, other sensitizers can remain, and FDA does not pre-approve cosmetics that way. Do not inflate the claim into a medical guarantee or use lacquer as primer.

distractorExplanations.a: All polish is chemicals. “Free” refers to a short list of omitted ingredients, not an empty bottle.
distractorExplanations.b: FDA does not pre-approve this class of cosmetics; an “X-free” sticker is not an allergy clearance.
distractorExplanations.d: Lacquer is not acrylic primer chemistry and will not create a proper enhancement bond.

prompt: A client with yellow, crumbling nails asks you to soak the fingers in household bleach “to kill fungus” before you apply enhancements. What is correct?

options.text: Surface-label bleach is acceptable as a finger soak
Laundry bleach use makes a nail soak equally safe
Floor-strength bleach can stand in as the dehydrator before product
Do not soak nails in bleach or treat suspected fungus with it

explanation: Household bleach is a surface or laundry chemical when the label and board allow those uses. It is not a medical antifungal and not a nail soak. Diagnosing or treating fungus is outside nail-technician scope; refuse the soak, do not enhance over untreated disease, and refer the client to a physician.

distractorExplanations.a: A hard-surface disinfectant label does not authorize soaking living nails; that is a chemical burn and scope error.
distractorExplanations.b: Towel laundry is not the same as skin contact. Linen use does not make a finger soak safe.
distractorExplanations.c: Dehydrator is a prep solvent for oil, not bleach. Floor mix on the plate is corrosive and off-protocol.
